steps.action: After reviewing time-reversal source imaging, the authors pose the open question of how the focal spot relates to the original source.
steps.quote: However, the question of the link between this focal spot and the details of the source of the earthquake still remains.

steps.action: Derived the time-reversed displacement from the representation theorem as a sum of monopole, dipole and sink contributions (eqs 2-8), showing the computable field lacks the sink term.
steps.quote: Let us first invoke the representation theorem (Masson et al. 2014), which reads in the frequency domain as

steps.action: Ran forward and backward SPECFEM2D simulations of an explosive point source in a homogeneous 2-D medium with a perfect circular mirror and recorded wavefields at three receivers and along a line.
steps.quote: To shed a first light on the similarities and discrepancies between u and utr

steps.action: Compared backward and forward displacements: they match far from the source, but within one wavelength of it the backward field shows a smooth focal spot instead of a discontinuity.
steps.quote: the backward displacement does not match the forward displacement: there is a smooth focal spot instead of a displacement discontinuity

steps.action: Proposed that point-source homogenization explains how two discontinuous fields (forward minus sink) combine into the smooth time-reversal wavefield.
steps.quote: In the following part, we show that it can be demonstrated thanks to the theory of point-source homogenization developed by Capdeville (2021).

steps.action: Restated the point-source homogenization theory (two-scale expansion, corrector, effective couple force; eqs 10-27) from the co-author's earlier work.
steps.quote: Capdeville (2021) recently applied homogenization to a point source.

steps.action: Checked the homogenized source for M = I with two filter values (epsilon0 = 1 and 0.5) against a reference displacement computed on a fine mesh at the source.
steps.quote: Fig. 7 shows that the corrector contributes to the displacement only near the source.

steps.action: Derived the main result (eq. 33): because the forward and sink correctors are equal, the time-reversal field equals the difference of the two zeroth-order homogenized fields.
steps.quote: This last equation is the main result of this paper.

steps.action: Computed u0 and us0 with epsilon0 = 0.5 in the simple 2-D case and compared their difference with the time-reversal field before, during and after focalization (Fig. 8).
Redefined the focal spot as an object extended in space and time, bounded by departure from the forward field and convergence to the negative sink field.
steps.quote: it allows us defining the focal spot as an extended object both in space and time

steps.action: Repeated the test with a non-isotropic moment tensor producing P and S waves (Fig. 9), on both x and z components.
steps.quote: matches utr(x, t) everywhere in space and time, which confirms eq. (33)

steps.action: Extended the derivation to an extended source discretized as multiple point sources (eq. 39).
steps.quote: This last equation is equivalent to (33) in the case of multiple point sources.

steps.action: Tested eq. (39) on a horizontal finite fault of four time-shifted point sources in the homogeneous medium (Fig. 10).
steps.quote: Despite this complexity, our theory holds

steps.action: Tested the result in a homogenized 2-D cross-section of the Groningen gas-field velocity model, with the source in the Zechstein salt (Figs 11-13).
steps.quote: Fig. 13 shows that having heterogeneity in the medium does not alter the result presented in Section 3.2.

steps.action: Kept the claim that the focal spot is the sum of two zeroth-order displacements generated by the homogenized point source, valid at all propagation times.
steps.quote: The relation is satisfied at all propagation times, including the focalization, which yields a new interpretation of the focal spot

steps.action: Compared backward simulations from a complete mirror and an incomplete two-well mirror for two explosive sources in the Groningen model; the incomplete-mirror focal spot is not covered by the theory.
steps.quote: In the current state of knowledge, such a focal spot is not a sum of two wavefields generated from the homogenization of the true source

steps.action: Argued from cited sensitivity studies and Groningen model uncertainties, without new simulation, that the derivation would degrade under velocity-model errors.
steps.quote: our derivation would degrade when the velocity model significantly deviates from the true earth

steps.action: Set the next refinement: include an incomplete mirror and medium uncertainties in the theory, toward downscaling focal spots to source mechanisms.
steps.quote: introducing an incomplete mirror and uncertainties on the propagation medium in our theory will be necessary

end.claim: With a complete mirror and a known lossless medium, the time-reversal wavefield, including the focal spot, equals the difference of the two zeroth-order wavefields (forward and sink) generated by the homogenized original point source.

decisive_move.sentence: The derivation of eq. (33), which shows that the forward and sink correctors cancel and leave only the two homogenized zeroth-order fields, creates the claim; the simulations illustrate it.

gates.evidence: After the derivation of eq. (33), the numerical experiments of Section 4 were designed to test it, and the match of u0 - us0 to utr could have failed (it is not claimed for the incomplete mirror, p. 1668). Nothing was fixed in advance; the first 2-D example (Section 2.2) was exploratory.

It demonstrates the smoothness of the time reversal wavefield, including the focal spot, in a [...] .

limits: All evidence is synthetic: 2-D spectral-element simulations, with no field data. The claim is labelled 'confirmed' because it faced numerical tests it could have failed, but no rival explanation is stated; the earlier theories are described as complements, so the status could also be read as a characterized theoretical relation. Composition is none_fits because the walk is derivation followed by numerical illustration in varied synthetic settings, which matches no listed composition. Sub-claims at other statuses: (1) validity for an incomplete mirror is not established; the focal spot only 'suggests' similar information (status none, p. 1668). (2) Degradation under velocity-model uncertainty is argued, not simulated (status none, p. 1668). (3) Validity in 3-D is asserted from the derivation but not simulated (p. 1666). (4) The claimed computational gain from a coarse mesh is explicitly not demonstrated (p. 1665). The choice of test moment tensors ('randomly chosen', 'chosen arbitrarily') is not motivated further. The extent of exploratory runs before the reported ones is not shown (inference: not knowable from the text). The code is available only on demand.

disagreements.target: Efforts to spike the focal spot (Kiser et al. 2011; Fukahata et al. 2014; Douma & Snieder 2014; Anderson et al. 2015; Bazargani & Snieder 2016; Nakata & Beroza 2016)
disagreements.support: Instead of sharpening the focal spot, the paper keeps it intact and upscales the source model so that smooth displacements fit it.
disagreements.quote: [...] it intact and proposes to upscale the source model in order to derive smooth displacements that fit the focal spot

disagreements.target: Velocity-uncertainty sensitivity results of Gajewski & Tessmer (2005) and Bazargani & Snieder (2016)
disagreements.support: The paper argues, without new simulation, that Groningen uncertainties do not keep the velocity range constant, so the focal-spot shift should be larger, and notes that those works did not study the wavefield inside the focal spot.
disagreements.quote: [...] that the impact on the focal spot position in time and space to be more significant than the one obtained by Gajewski [...]
